Core Concept

Pipeline Triggers: Automatic vs. Manual

Understanding how your CI/CD pipelines are initiated

Automatic Triggers

  • •Initiated by code changes like git push.
  • •Also triggered by new merge requests or tags.
  • •Can be scheduled to run at specific times.
  • •Ensures continuous integration and immediate feedback.
Example Scenario

A developer pushes new code to a feature branch, automatically starting a test pipeline.

Manual Triggers

  • •Explicitly started from the GitLab UI.
  • •Configured using when: manual in .gitlab-ci.yml.
  • •Ideal for sensitive operations like production deployments.
  • •Requires human approval or specific conditions.
Use Case

A release manager manually triggers a production deployment after all tests pass and approvals are met.

Key Takeaway

Choosing the right trigger type ensures pipelines run efficiently and securely, aligning with your project's operational needs.

screens.title: The Power of Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Automatic triggers are the backbone of continuous integration, ensuring that every code change is immediately validated. The most common trigger is a git push to your repository. Whenever you commit changes and push them to any branch, GitLab automatically detects your. gitlab-ci. yml file and initiates a new pipeline run for that specific commit. This immediate feedback loop is invaluable for catching issues early in the development cycle. Beyond simple pushes, pipelines can also be triggered by creating a new merge request, which is often used to run pre-merge checks like code style validation or unit tests. Pushing a tag, typically used for marking releases, can also trigger pipelines for tasks like building release artifacts or publishing to registries. Furthermore, for recurring tasks such as nightly builds, security scans, or data synchronization, pipelines can be configured to run on a predefined schedule. This ensures that even without direct code changes, your project remains healthy and up-to-date. Understanding these automatic triggers helps you design a truly hands-off and efficient CI/CD process. Module 3›Chapter 2.3›Manual Triggers
Manual Triggers

Controlling Execution with Manual Jobs

How to configure and run jobs that require human approval

Manual Trigger Options

  • •Directly from GitLab UI: CI/CD > Pipelines > Run pipeline.
  • •Configure a job with when: manual in .gitlab-ci.yml.
  • •Useful for sensitive operations like production deployments.
Pro-Tip

Combine when: manual with allow_failure: false for critical jobs to ensure pipeline failure on manual job errors.

deploy_to_production:
  stage: deploy
  image: alpine/git:latest
  script:
    - echo "Initiating production deployment..."
  rules:
    - if: '$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == "main"'
      when: manual # This job will only run if manually triggered
      allow_failure: false # If it fails, the pipeline will be marked as failed
    - when: never # Otherwise, don't include this job
Key Takeaway

Manual jobs are crucial for controlled, human-approved steps in your CI/CD workflow, especially for sensitive operations.

screens.title: The Job Log: Your Debugging Hub
screens.narratorSegment: When a pipeline job fails, your first and most critical stop for debugging is the job log. Each job in the pipeline graph is clickable, and clicking on it will take you to its individual job page. This page is where you'll find the job's current status, details about the runner it executed on, and most importantly, the comprehensive job log. The job log is a detailed, chronological output of every command executed by the job, including both its standard output and any standard error messages. Think of it as a complete transcript of what happened during the job's execution. When a job fails, the log will typically highlight the exact command that failed and provide any error messages produced by that command or the system. This raw output is invaluable because it shows you precisely what the runner was trying to do and where it encountered a problem. Learning to read and interpret these logs effectively is the cornerstone of efficient CI/CD debugging, allowing you to quickly diagnose and resolve issues. It's a skill that will save you countless hours of frustration.

screens.title: Diagnosing Pipeline Failures (Part 1)
screens.narratorSegment: When a pipeline job fails, it can be frustrating, but many issues stem from common failure points that are relatively easy to diagnose once you know what to look for. One of the first things GitLab checks is the syntax of your. gitlab-ci. yml file. If there are any YAML linting errors, GitLab will usually catch these even before the pipeline fully starts, giving you a clear 'YAML linting failed' message. This is a quick fix, often just a misplaced space or incorrect indentation. Another very common issue is incorrect commands within your script block. A simple typo in a command like npm install or an incorrect file path can cause the shell command to fail, leading to a job failure. Always double-check your commands and paths. Finally, missing dependencies are a frequent culprit. If your specified Docker image doesn't contain a required tool like git, docker, or python, or if your before underscore script fails to install a necessary package, subsequent commands will inevitably fail. This highlights the importance of choosing the right base image and ensuring all prerequisites are met. Understanding these initial failure points will significantly speed up your debugging process.

A simple typo in a command like npm install or an incorrect file path can cause the shell command to fail, leading to a job failure. Always double-check your commands and paths. Finally, missing dependencies are a frequent culprit. If your specified Docker image doesn't contain a required tool like git, docker, or python, or if your before underscore script fails to install a necessary package, subsequent commands will inevitably fail. This highlights the importance of choosing the right base image and ensuring all prerequisites are met. Understanding these initial failure points will significantly speed up your debugging process.

Common Issues

Diagnosing Pipeline Failures (Part 1)

Identifying frequent causes of CI/CD job errors

YAML Syntax Errors

Incorrect indentation or structure in .gitlab-ci.yml often leads to "YAML linting failed" errors before execution.

Incorrect Script Commands

Typos, wrong arguments, or incorrect paths in your script block will cause shell commands to fail.

Missing Dependencies

The Docker image might lack required tools (e.g., Node.js, Python) or before_script failed to install packages.

Key Takeaway

Always check YAML syntax, script commands, and ensure all necessary dependencies are available in your job's environment.

screens.title: Diagnosing Pipeline Failures (Part 2)
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the more straightforward issues, pipeline failures can also stem from more subtle problems related to the execution environment or data flow. Environment issues are a common culprit. This could involve incorrect environment variables that your script relies on, network connectivity problems preventing access to external services, or insufficient permissions on the GitLab Runner itself. These issues often manifest as 'permission denied' errors or timeouts, and require careful inspection of the job log and potentially the runner's configuration. Another area to watch out for is artifacts issues. If a job produces files that are needed by a subsequent job, but these files are not correctly declared as artifacts or the downstream job has incorrect dependencies, then the consuming job will fail due to missing files. This highlights the importance of understanding how artifacts are passed between jobs. Debugging these types of failures often requires a deeper understanding of the GitLab CI/CD execution model and careful attention to the details in your. gitlab-ci. yml configuration. By systematically checking these potential problem areas, you can efficiently narrow down the cause of even complex pipeline failures.

screens.title: Effective Troubleshooting with Job Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Now that you know where to find the job logs and common failure points, let's dive into practical debugging strategies. The first rule of thumb is to carefully read the job log from bottom to top. Often, the last few lines before the job fails contain the critical error message. Don't just skim; look for keywords like 'error', 'failed', 'permission denied', or 'command not found'. To gain more insight into your script's execution, you can add echo statements to print variable values or messages at different points in your script. Similarly, ls -la commands can be invaluable for inspecting file paths and verifying if expected files or directories exist at a given stage. For shell scripts, a powerful trick is to add set -ex at the beginning of your script block. set -e ensures that the script exits immediately if any command fails, preventing subsequent commands from running and potentially masking the original error. set -x prints each command before it's executed, providing a detailed trace of exactly what the script was trying to do. This verbose output can be a lifesaver for complex scripts, giving you a step-by-step breakdown of the execution flow and helping you pinpoint the exact line where things went wrong. These strategies, combined with careful log analysis, will significantly enhance your debugging capabilities.

Module 3›Chapter 2.3›Debugging Strategies
Debugging Strategies

Effective Troubleshooting with Job Logs

Practical techniques for pinpointing and resolving failures

Read Logs Carefully

Start from the bottom of the log and work upwards; the last few lines often contain the critical error message.

Add Debugging Commands

Use echo to print variable values and ls -la to inspect file paths at different points in your script.

Pro-Tip

For shell scripts, add set -ex at the beginning of your script to exit on error and print commands before execution.

debug_job:
  stage: debug
  image: alpine/git:latest
  script:
    - set -ex # Exit on error, print commands
    - echo "Debugging environment..."
    - ls -la /app # Check if /app directory exists
    - cat /app/config.txt || true # Try to read a file, continue if not found
    - my_non_existent_command # This command will fail and stop the script
    - echo "This line will not be reached."
Key Takeaway

Leverage set -ex and strategic logging to gain deep visibility into script execution and quickly identify failure points.

screens.title: Safeguarding Sensitive Information
screens.narratorSegment: As you become more proficient in configuring and debugging pipelines, it's absolutely critical to adopt a fundamental security best practice: never commit sensitive information directly into your. gitlab-ci. yml file or your repository. This includes A P I keys, database credentials, private tokens, or any other confidential data. Exposing such information, even in private repositories, poses a significant security risk. Instead, GitLab provides a robust mechanism called CI/CD variables. These variables allow you to securely store sensitive data at the project, group, or even instance level. They can be masked, preventing their values from appearing in job logs, and protected, meaning they are only available in pipelines running on protected branches or tags. While we'll delve deeper into CI/CD variables in a later module, it's crucial to understand this principle from the start. Always use these secure variables for any sensitive configuration values. This practice not only protects your credentials but also makes your pipelines more flexible and reusable across different environments without hardcoding secrets. Adopting this early will save you from potential security vulnerabilities down the line. It's your window into the entire CI/CD process. Crucially, the Job Log is the detailed output of commands executed by a job, including standard output and error messages, making it indispensable for debugging. When something goes wrong, the log tells the story. Finally, we covered Debugging Strategies, which are techniques like carefully reading logs, adding echo statements, using ls -la to inspect files, and employing set -ex in shell scripts to trace execution and identify failures. These practical methods empower you to efficiently resolve issues. These concepts collectively provide you with the skills to not only run pipelines but also to confidently diagnose and fix any problems that arise, ensuring your CI/CD system remains robust and reliable.
